title: Uji - Time Being
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona and Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: The speaker's main teaching is that time is not separate from the present moment, but rather an integral part of it. This means that every moment is connected to and encompasses all of existence, past, present, and future, and that there is no distinction between these concepts. By letting go of our worries and judgments about time, we can appreciate the present moment as it truly is, unencumbered by our perceptions of past or future.

sentences.text: Boundlessness is one of the core concepts of Buddhism.
While I perceive the world from the perspective of me, examining more closely, people I see as other are not separate from me.
The awakened way of living is to be mindful of and comfortable with both perspectives: both this story of a separate self and the fundamental truth of interconnection.
This month we have been studying the teachings of the founder of Soto Zen, Eihei Dogen.
In his fascical writing called *Uji*, translated as time being, he says the same concept of boundlessness applies to the dimension of time too.
While we only perceive this present moment, the distinction from all other moments is fuzzy.
Just as our self is not separate from other beings, this moment is not separate from history or future.
That is why we invited you to closely study the experience of time as we sat down in meditation.
For this examination, Kate and I have decided to look at the teachings of Brad Warner.
Mr.
Warner is a Buddhist teacher in Los Angeles who studied under Tim McCarthy and Gudo Nishijima Roshi.
He was ordained in Japan and plays bass in a punk band.
He is noted for humor and accessible paraphrasing of Zen teachings.
While Warner himself wouldn't consider his book a true translation, we found him to be surprisingly faithful to the original structure of the text.

Warner describes this *Uji* section as psychedelic Dogen, because there is the opportunity for a mind-altering experience, but of a corrective nature—seeing past some errors and assumptions in everyday perception and cognition.
Why is Dogen so difficult to understand sometimes?
One of the problems is the attempt to use intellectual understanding to penetrate errors and assumptions that misdirect intellectual understanding.
It's like trying to wipe a smudge of grease off your glasses by rubbing your finger across it.
Warner quotes his teacher Nishijima as identifying four different lenses that Dogen is switching between when he writes about a topic.
Note that the first two of those lenses are bifurcated study of opposites.
So if we try to understand one of his texts looking through a single lens, no wonder we're confused.
For me personally, Dogen's writings are comforting, as I recognize a beautiful truth that the universe is unfolding just as it should and I have nothing to worry about.
Though of course I have plenty of actions to perform.
I have faith in non-understanding.
It helps to let go of judgments.
Sometimes Dogen makes confrontational statements such as, "only an unenlightened fool would pursue such a path."
It's so easy to fall into the trap of an unenlightened fool.
Well, that's bad.
I don't want to be that.
But if you're willing to be the idiot when you read Dogen, you can walk with him on both sides of the road at once.
Non-understanding is closer to beyond understanding than understanding is.
Thank you.

If time is being, root weevils are time.
